I built the audit tool that didn't exist

UX copy was shipping to production with zero quality checks. No tool could fix it. So I defined the scoring model, designed the system, and built the Chrome extension myself — as a UX writer with no engineering background.

01
The Problem

Copy shipped. Nobody checked.

"Error messages are vague. Sentences are too long. Copy sounds like it was written by a system, not a person. By the time someone notices, it's already live."

Birdeye ships features to staging constantly. The design review process checks UI, interaction, and accessibility. But UX writing quality — the actual clarity of the words on the screen — had no systematic check. It was entirely dependent on whoever happened to notice something was off.

This isn't a people problem. It's a tooling problem. There was no instrument designed for this job. The tools that existed were built for different audiences with different needs.

02
My Role

One person. Every layer.

I'm a UX Writer. Not an engineer. I wrote this case study, designed the scoring model, and directed every line of code — using vibe coding with Cursor AI and Claude as my engineering pair. I had no developer. No tester. No design partner.

What solo actually means

I discovered the problem, researched the domain (readability science, passive voice detection, browser extension architecture), wrote five Jira task documents defining the technical specification, designed the UI, defined the scoring logic with academic citations, and shipped a working Chrome extension. The code was generated by AI. Every decision was mine.

The Solution

One click. Full UX writing audit.

The Birdeye UXW Auditor is a Chrome extension that runs directly on live deployed product pages. It reads the rendered DOM, filters noise, runs the copy through a four-signal scoring engine, and returns a structured quality report in seconds.

The Engine

How the scoring model was built

This is the part that makes the tool defensible. Before writing a single line of code, I spent weeks in research defining what a UX clarity score should actually measure — and why. Every weight, every threshold, every rule is cited.

The four signals — and why they're weighted this way

35%
Flesch Reading Ease
The single strongest predictor of comprehension. Developed for the Associated Press in the 1940s, validated over decades across audiences. Higher score = easier to read. Target for Birdeye B2B: 60+.
25%
Sentence Complexity
Long sentences are the most common UX writing failure in B2B products. Nielsen Norman eye-tracking research shows users read only 20–28% of words on a page. Every word over 25 is a bet against the user continuing.
25%
Passive Voice Rate
Passive voice by habit signals unclear, system-oriented writing. It removes accountability, adds cognitive friction, and makes users work harder to understand who does what. Over 15% is a red flag.
15%
FK Grade Level
Supporting signal only. Confirms or challenges the Reading Ease score. Gets 15% because it overlaps significantly with signal 1 — giving it more would double-count the same underlying data.

The scoring formula

UX Clarity Score Formula
// Each signal produces a sub-score from 0–100
// Weights are based on research-backed signal priority

UX Clarity Score =
  (Flesch Reading Ease  × 0.35) +
  (Sentence Sub-score   × 0.25) +
  (Passive Voice Score  × 0.25) +
  (FK Grade Sub-score   × 0.15)

// Flesch Reading Ease formula:
Flesch RE = 206.835 - (1.015 × avg_words_per_sentence)
                   - (84.6  × avg_syllables_per_word)

// Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level:
FK Grade = (0.39 × avg_words_per_sentence)
         + (11.8 × avg_syllables_per_word)
         - 15.59

Score bands and what they mean

70 – 100  ·  GOOD
Copy meets clarity standards. No urgent action. Ship it.
50 – 69  ·  NEEDS REVIEW
Specific signals failing. Assign to content designer to address before release.
0 – 49  ·  POOR
Significant communication debt. Prioritise for structured rewrite in next sprint.

Readability thresholds — calibrated for B2B SaaS

Setting thresholds is not a guess. I cross-referenced Nielsen Norman Group, UX Content Collective, and real-world benchmarks. The key insight: even professional B2B users prefer plain language — because they scan, not read.

Flesch Reading Ease
60 and above GOOD
40 – 59 REVIEW
Below 40 POOR
Benchmark: Reader's Digest ~65 · Time Magazine ~52 · Harvard Law Review ~30
FK Grade Level
Grade 8 or below GOOD
Grade 9 – 11 REVIEW
Grade 12+ POOR
Source: NNG, American Press Institute, B2B SaaS conventions research

How passive voice detection actually works

I evaluated three approaches: full NLP parsing (too heavy for a browser extension), spaCy dependency parsing (requires a backend, not viable), and rule-based pattern matching. Rule-based is what every production tool in this space uses — and it's what I built.

Passive Voice Detection — Step by Step
⚑ Passive — flagged

The report was generated by the system.

Birdeye sends responses automatically.

Long sentence thresholds — research-backed

The American Press Institute found that comprehension drops below 10% when average sentence length hits 43 words. I used that research to set conservative thresholds with two tiers.

>25 words
Warning — sentence is getting long. Review it.
>35 words
Fail — sentence is too long. Must be rewritten before release.
>60 words
Noise — filtered out. This is almost certainly user-generated data, not product copy.

Technical architecture — what each file does

.json
manifest.json
The badge. Tells Chrome what permissions the extension needs and what files to load.
.js
content.js
The worker. Injected into every page. Extracts text, runs detection logic, responds to messages from popup.
.html
popup.html
The UI shell. Renders the score, signals, and findings when you click the extension icon.
.css
popup.css
Birdeye brand identity. Navy header, blue CTA, pill grid, collapsible findings.
.js
popup.js
Popup logic. Sends audit message, renders findings, handles export and highlight.

Click-to-highlight — how the page feedback works

Every finding in the popup is clickable. When you click, the extension finds the flagged text on the page, wraps it in a yellow highlight, and scrolls to it. It disappears after 3 seconds — no clutter.

1
User clicks a finding in the popup panel
2
Extension searches for the first 4 words of that finding in the live DOM
3
Wraps it in a <span> with background: #FFF176 · outline: 2px solid #F9A825
4
scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'center' }) — scroll to it
5
Highlight auto-removes after 3,000ms — no permanent DOM changes
04
Export System

The report is the deliverable.

An audit only creates value if the findings travel. Every audit exports two files simultaneously — a structured JSON for developers and future dashboards, and a flat CSV for PMs to paste directly into Jira. The format was designed by studying how Google Lighthouse and Microsoft's Accessibility Insights structure their exports.

Export PDF and Export CSV — both download simultaneously

The exported PDF report — full score breakdown, all four signals, and every finding verbatim

05
Build Process

How I went from spec to working extension

Every build decision started with a Jira task document. Before writing a prompt for Cursor, I wrote a document explaining the decision, the research behind it, and the exact rule to implement. The code was a downstream output of the thinking.

The proof-of-concept first

The very first task (BIRD-183315) wasn't about scoring. It was a proof of concept: can the extension reliably extract visible text off a live Birdeye page? The rule: if it couldn't print clean product copy to the DevTools console with a [UXW] prefix, nothing else gets built. That gate passed. Then the scoring engine was built on top of a confirmed foundation.

The five technical documents I wrote before any code

BIRD-183305
Define Scoring Weights
Research + rationale for the 35/25/25/15 weight split. Cited NNG, Acrolinx, UX Content Collective. Locked in before any code was written.
BIRD-183306
Set Readability Thresholds
What does "good" look like specifically for B2B SaaS? Researched consumer vs enterprise benchmarks. Defined what grade 8 means in practice for Birdeye's professional user base.
BIRD-183307
Passive Voice Rules + Long Sentence Limits
Evaluated three detection approaches. Chose rule-based pattern matching. Defined the exact regex logic. Established the 25/35/60-word sentence tiers with American Press Institute citation.
BIRD-183308
Define Export Format
Studied Google Lighthouse and Accessibility Insights export structures. Mapped three user types (UX writer, PM, design lead) to their specific report needs. Defined JSON and CSV schemas.
BIRD-183315
Console Log Proof of Concept
Smallest possible test: can the extension read visible text from a live page? Defined visibility rules, exclusion logic, and what clean output looks like. Gate for starting Story 2.
